newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Norilsk to meet, consider rocky road to recovery.
newsitem.headline: Norilsk to meet, consider rocky road to recovery.

text.p: A restructuring plan aimed at dragging Russia's mining giant Norilsk Nickel NKEL.RTS into the 21st century and ridding it of mountainous debts will top the agenda when the group's board of directors meets Thursday.
The board, and shareholders of its flagship metals combine who are also due to meet, are likely to consider plans to issue shares or bonds to address the problem of debts to the state.
"This question will be looked at (on Thursday)," said Anatoly Komrakov, Moscow-based spokesman for parent RAO Norilsky Nikel. "But I can't say when it will definitely be decided."

A company official last month said the group may issue level-one American Depositary Receipts by July. A company statement also said the flagship combine would issue shares or bonds to help reduce debts.
One option being considered is to double the capital of the flagship plant and transfer a majority stake to the government.

Norilsk is one of Russia's 15 biggest corporate tax debtors, and is part of a government plan to restructure debts of those companies by issuing shares or bonds to be held by the government while the tax arrears are paid off.
In March Norilsk's debts to combine workers were 900 billion roubles ($156.3 million), with another 1.2 trillion owed to various budgets.

While addressing the company's debt burden is the most pressing concern for board and shareholders now, equally important in the long term is hiving off Norilsk's huge non-core activities and enormous social outlays.
The metals combine shoulders the burden of supporting a community of 300,000 in the Arctic town built around it, less than half of whom actually appear on the company payroll.
Last month it announced it would not replace 10,000 employees who had applied to leave this year, reducing the workforce by around eight percent.
The combine also funds a construction arm, social and community infrastructure, accommodation and other enterprises in the town of Norilsk not directly related to production.
Komrakov said the combine had gone some way towards separating these enterprises from the main business.

"The mayor of the town (Norilsk) has already agreed in principle to take on around 130 enterprises, including cafes and restaurants," Komrakov said. "Yes, even restaurants have been appearing on the combine's balance sheets -- it's simply crazy."
The combine plans to create four units to separate results related to metal production from those related to non-core activities like construction and housing.
The combine already has separate mining, refining and construction arms, and plans to create a fourth dealing with housing and community services.
"The division will in no way touch the way metals are produced and exported, but only the effectiveness and efficiency of the separate entities," Komrakov said.
He also said the company was sticking to a wage payment deal struck with unions. The schedule was agreed between workers and management to avert strike action threatened in March and April.

Norilsk's restructuring plan is the brainchild of commercial bank Uneximbank, which controls a 38 percent stake in the parent group and 51 percent of its voting shares. Details of the company's other shareholders were not immediately available.
If the restructuring plan succeeds, cash should eventually be freed up for re-building a depleted ore base and modernising refining techniques -- the basic functions on which the group depends.

"In the last few years average ore grades at the huge Oktyabrsky mine have been on a precipitous downward path due to the lack of investment in mine development," said Jim Lennon of Macquarie Equities in London.
"I think it is going to be a struggle and they face enormous challenges, but the bottom line is that there is a phenomenal resource. Yes, I think they will eventually get there," he said.

The flagship metals combine, situated in the Arctic town of Norilsk that was built around the company, is the backbone of the group, accounting for 70 percent of its overall metals output and lying close to enormous mineral deposits.
Norilsk is one of the world's biggest suppliers of nickel, cobalt, platinum and palladium, and a major supplier of copper.

The Norilsk group produced 177,185 tonnes in 1996, down from 180,100 in 1995. It produced 340,000 tonnes of copper and 3,151 tonnes of cobalt, not to mention huge volumes of platinum and palladium, details of which are a closely-guarded state secret.
